summary: Round 3. F7 (the sixth at-most-once copy) is genuinely fixed and I found no seventh: a whole-tree grep for at-most-once / idempoten / safe-retry / exactly-once outside docs/research returns only correct uses. The seven copies of the retry fact (Sequencer contract section, Sequencer failure-and-retry paragraph, Sequencer @throws, CommitRequest class javadoc, FakeSequencer javadoc, FakeSequencerTest assertion description, backlog row) are mutually consistent and all say idempotency is M4.10 and does not hold. F8, F9, F10, F11 verified fixed; F9's Map.copyOf claim verified empirically on Java 25.0.4 (null key and null value both NPE), so dropping the loop's null checks weakens nothing, and anEmptyOrNonPositiveRecordCountIsRefused still passes and still discriminates. F2 re-measured independently: 12 of 12 fresh JVMs kill the sort-deletion mutation at six keys. GATE_SCOPE=full check-module ok (8 modules); suite 432 tests, 0 failures, 0 errors, 0 skipped, sequencer 17 -- the backlog row's numbers are true. Cost lens clean: commit() is structurally per-segment (one segmentKey per request, many streams in one recordCounts map), no I/O anywhere in the diff, nothing that scales with records, shards, partitions or indices. Round-3 call judged sound: architecture.md:68 forbids splitting the fake out of the seam commit, and at 6 files / ~590 lines mostly javadoc the round-2 finding was a prose contradiction rather than a symptom of size, so rule 12's 'it means the commit is too big' diagnosis does not apply and neither of its two remedies fits. Five minors below; none blocks.

findings.title: The contract is silent on concurrency, and the fake asserts a locking property of the real implementation that does not exist
findings.surviving_mutation: n/a -- contract gap. FakeSequencer's javadoc says 'NOT thread-safe, and deliberately so -- a test that needs concurrency is testing the real implementation's locking, not this. The real one is M4.2 onward.' The real one is ingest/src/main/java/binjava/ingest/CommitLog.java, which holds `private final Map<RunKey, Long> nextOffsets = new HashMap<>()` and a plain `long nextSequence` with no synchronization anywhere. Serialisation today comes from the CALLER: DefaultIngest.java:65 holds a ReentrantLock and calls log.commit inside flushLocked. So the fake attributes to the implementation a property the caller currently owns, and the interface -- whose stated contract is this task's entire deliverable -- never says which side owns it.
findings.failure_scenario: The task asks whether M4.2 can build against this seam without inventing a decision. On threading it cannot: M4.2 is specified as a PURE move of CommitLog with no behaviour change, so it will place an unsynchronised class behind an interface that does not require thread-safety, guided by a fake that says the implementation locks. The moment a second caller thread appears -- M4.7's batching window, or M5's forwarded commits arriving on the peer-mesh threads rather than under DefaultIngest's flush lock -- two concurrent commits race on nextOffsets/nextSequence and can hand the same offset to two different records. That is a silent I2 violation ('a committed offset is never reassigned'), the invariant architecture.md calls load-bearing for OpenSearch replica convergence, and no test catches it because the contract never demanded thread-safety and the fake explicitly declines to model it. One sentence on the interface -- implementations must be safe for concurrent commit, or callers must serialise -- closes it; that sentence belongs either here or in M4.2's commit, and M4.2 should not be left to invent it silently.
findings.remedy: State the threading obligation on Sequencer.commit, and correct FakeSequencer's 'the real implementation's locking' to name whoever actually owns serialisation.

findings.title: F11's new close() clause falsifies the fake's blanket conformance claim, and close is missing from the fake's own 'does NOT model' list -- the same one-copy-fixed-duplicate-missed pattern
findings.surviving_mutation: n/a -- documentation duplicate. The interface now says 'After close a commit must fail rather than silently succeed' and discloses that the fake deviates. FakeSequencer's own javadoc still opens with 'IT HONOURS THE SAME CONTRACT THE INTERFACE STATES, and its own tests pin it there. A fake that quietly differs is worse than no fake at all', which is now false for close, and its explicit 'What this fake does NOT model, on purpose' list (durability, leases, epochs, sealing, idempotency) does not mention close. No test in FakeSequencerTest exercises commit-after-close in either direction.
findings.failure_scenario: A test author reads the fake, not the interface -- that is what a fake is for. M4.12 builds the fault-injecting simulation with MANY LOGICAL PODS driven through this seam; a seed that models a lease loss or a shutdown by closing a sequencer and continuing to commit through it goes green against the fake, while the real implementation is contractually required to throw. The simulation then certifies a failover behaviour the system does not have, which is exactly the divergence the fake's own javadoc says is worse than having no fake. Adding 'and, for now, post-close refusal' to the not-modelled list is the whole fix.
findings.remedy: Add close to FakeSequencer's not-modelled list, or soften the blanket conformance sentence so the two copies agree.

findings.title: 'the delta is durable ... so a caller may acknowledge the write (FR-4)' licenses an ack on the delta's own durability alone, which is not what I5 requires
findings.surviving_mutation: n/a -- contract statement. I5 (architecture.md): 'No acknowledged commit exists beyond a SEAL in its own chain -- a commit is acked only after every lower-numbered write is confirmed.' The contract section conditions the ack on this delta's durability and never mentions the lower-numbered writes.
findings.failure_scenario: M4.11 exists to establish I5 and its own backlog row warns that 'today's CommitLog is strictly serial and so satisfies I5 BY ACCIDENT', and M4.0's row quotes the corpus calling I5 'the one a plausible invariant-respecting implementation violates by accident'. An implementer who pipelines for throughput -- which M4.11 explicitly permits -- and returns from commit(N) as soon as N's own conditional PUT is confirmed satisfies the letter of this javadoc while commit(N-1) is still in flight; the caller acks on return, per this sentence, and I5 is broken. The seam is the one place that obligation can be stated once for every implementation. Not raised higher because I5 binds every implementation via architecture.md whether or not the javadoc restates it, and M4.11's row carries the guard.
findings.remedy: One clause on commit: returning normally means the ack is safe under I5, i.e. every lower-numbered write in the chain is confirmed.

findings.title: 'Six keys drops the escape to 1 in 720' is an unmeasured number resting on a uniformity assumption that Map.copyOf does not satisfy
findings.surviving_mutation: n/a -- claim accuracy. Map.copyOf's iteration order is the probe order of a salted open-addressed table, not a uniform random permutation of the keys, so 1/n! does not follow. Measured here, 12 fresh JVMs over exactly this fixture (compiled against format's RunKey, printing Map.copyOf's key order): six keys produced only 5 distinct orders and the sorted order never appeared -- 12/12 KILLED, so the FIX IS GOOD and better than claimed. The same probe on the old three-key fixture escaped in 4 of 12 runs, roughly 1 in 3, not the 1 in 6 the comment repeats from round 2's suggestion.
findings.failure_scenario: The comment is the durable record of why this test uses six streams, and a later author will reuse its arithmetic -- 'three keys is only 1 in 6, that is fine for a small test' -- on the next ordering assertion in this codebase, understating the real escape rate by about a factor of two in the case I measured. Non-negotiable 4 is about not stating numbers that were not measured; this one was inherited from a review suggestion and then written into the tree as fact. Say what was measured (N of N fresh JVMs killed the mutation) rather than a derived probability, since the distribution is salted, structured and not enumerable.
findings.remedy: Replace the 1-in-720 arithmetic with the measurement actually taken.

findings.title: The row records rounds 1 and 2 in detail but never says the two-round cap was exceeded, or why splitting was rejected
findings.surviving_mutation: n/a. review.md rule 12 caps review at two rounds and says a blocking finding in round two means the commit is too big -- split it. This task took three. The row narrates both earlier rounds' findings but contains no sentence saying the cap was passed or on what grounds.
findings.failure_scenario: The backlog is the durable record and rule 12's own text is a measured lesson (M-1.1: five rounds, every extra round finding defects in the previous round's fix). A row that reads as a normal two-round task sets the precedent that a third round is unremarkable, and the next author with a round-2 major does the same without deciding anything. The grounds here are good and take one sentence -- architecture.md:68 requires the fake in the seam's own commit so the split rule 12 prescribes is forbidden, and the round-2 finding was a prose contradiction in a 6-file commit rather than a symptom of size -- which also surfaces the real gap: rule 12 offers only 'split' or 'argue' and neither fits a small commit whose round-2 finding is a doc defect. Worth a sentence in the commit body, and arguably a backlog row against review.md.
findings.remedy: One sentence in the row or the commit body recording the cap breach and why splitting was not available.

findings.title: The @return says what will stop being true at M4.7 but not what IS true today, and names the missing field a reader could be tempted to add
findings.surviving_mutation: n/a -- contract gap. F10's remedy correctly stopped over-promising RunKey selection and states the bound. What it does not say is that until M4.7 lands, one request produces one delta and the whole delta IS this caller's, which is the only thing a caller written between now and M4.7 can act on.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller must ack the producer per FR-4 and therefore must know which offsets are its own. Reading this, an implementor learns only that treating the delta as its own will be wrong later and that 'neither CommitDelta nor RunCommit carries pod attribution' -- which reads as an invitation to add the field. CommitDelta is a wire format (its own javadoc says so, non-negotiable 8), so adding pod attribution now would be a format change made rows ahead of the milestone that owns the decision, exactly the hazard M4.3's row spells out for the lease's checkpoint pointer. The sentence 'How a caller learns which offsets are its own is M4.7's to settle' is what keeps this a minor rather than a major; saying what holds today would close it.
findings.remedy: Add that until M4.7 one request yields one delta and every run in it is this caller's.

verified_this_round: F7 fixed and no seventh copy: grep -rniE 'at[- ]most[- ]once|idempoten|safe to retry|retry is safe|exactly.once|replay' across the whole tree excluding docs/research returns no unmarked claim; the only at-most-once outside the sequencer is ingest/Ingest.java:51 about consuming a records stream, a different subject.
The seven copies of the retry fact are mutually consistent and every one marks idempotency as M4.10 and not yet true.

F8: the -/ reason now matches format/SegmentKey.java:71-82 verbatim in substance (the header-length marker is parsed on those separators); the inherited-not-intrinsic framing and the POD_NAME consequence are both accurate.

F9: Map.copyOf now precedes both the isEmpty check and the positivity loop. Verified empirically on Java 25.0.4 that Map.copyOf throws NPE for a null key and for a null value, so the dropped loop null-checks were unreachable and nothing was weakened. anEmptyOrNonPositiveRecordCountIsRefused still discriminates both arms (Map.of -> isEmpty -> IAE; Map.of(key,0) -> loop -> IAE).
F10: no longer over-promises; see G6 for what it still omits.

F11: does not pre-empt M4.3 -- no TTL value is hardcoded and the ~10 s figure is ADR-0007's own (decisions/0007:45); release-on-close is a consequence of the ADR, not a lease mechanism. It does contradict FakeSequencer's blanket claim -- G2.

F2 re-measured independently in 12 fresh JVMs against the exact six-key fixture: 12/12 kill the sort-deletion mutation. The three-key fixture escaped 4/12. Fix confirmed; only the stated probability is off -- G4.

F1 left unpinned is acceptable: check-mutants.sh does not exist (testing.md rule 9 lands in M0.14 and calls both floors aspirations until their scripts are in scripts/), so a baselines/mutants.txt line would pin nothing today and baselines/ has no such file. But do NOT take the other option and delete the claim from the comment: the property is real -- it is what makes the record's own invariant hold against a caller mutating between check and copy -- and it IS deterministically testable, contrary to round 2's inconclusive attempt, with a Map whose entrySet() yields a valid entry on the read Map.copyOf makes and an invalid one on the read the validation loop makes. Under copy-first the record is valid; under validate-then-copy it holds a non-positive count. Better as a backlog row than as a deletion.
GATE_SCOPE=full ./scripts/check-module.sh: ok, 8 modules, rule5 tested 4, rule2 tested 2.
./gradlew test green; counted from the JUnit XML: 432 tests, 0 failures, 0 errors, 0 skipped, sequencer 17. The backlog row's numbers are true.

Cost: commit() is structurally per-segment (one segmentKey, many streams in one recordCounts map), no store call anywhere in the diff, no idle-path request, no LIST. Request rate follows segments, not records/shards/partitions/indices.

Round-3 call sound: architecture.md:68 requires every seam's fake in the same commit, so rule 12's split remedy is unavailable, and the round-2 finding was a doc contradiction in a 6-file mostly-javadoc commit rather than evidence of size. Recording that reasoning is G5.
